description: Question: why are LEDs and laser diodes made of III-V and II-VI compounds (GaAs, InP, GaN, ZnSe) and not of silicon, the best-understood semiconductor there is? Data: every stable element and binary compound with a band gap and at most 4 atoms per cell in Alexandria (PBE density-functional calculations, Ruhr University Bochum, via its keyless OPTIMADE API): the fundamental gap and the smallest direct gap; and PubChem's periodic table for each element's valence electrons and electronegativity. Steps: the gap is direct when the smallest vertical gap equals the fundamental one (within 0.005 eV); each material gets a family from its elements' valences (III-V: 3 and 5 in a 1:1 compound; II-VI and I-VII split by whether the metal has a full d shell, Zn/Cd/Hg and Cu/Ag, or is an alkaline-earth/alkali metal); shares of direct gaps per family with Wilson 95% intervals; a two-proportion z-test of III-V and II-VI against the rest. Aha: an electron in an indirect-gap material (Si: the direct gap is about 1.9 eV above the fundamental one) can only fall across the gap if a lattice vibration takes up its momentum, so it emits light a million times more slowly than it loses its energy as heat; in GaAs or GaN the band edges line up and a photon is emitted directly. Caveats: PBE underestimates band gaps by 30 to 100% (Si 0.65 eV here against 1.12 measured; GaAs 0.20 against 1.42), and Ge, InAs and InSb come out metallic and are missing; the direct/indirect character is more robust than the value but near-direct materials (GaP, margin 0.02 eV) can flip; families with few members have wide intervals; the photon wavelengths in the tooltips use PBE gaps and are too long. Next: drill into III-V (why AlAs and GaP are indirect), expand to alloys (AlGaAs, GaAsP turn indirect at a crossover composition) and to measured gaps.
name: Direct and indirect band gaps: why LEDs are not silicon
